sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language models to robot control (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b,a; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026). common design keeps the autoregressive next-token prediction of the backbone: an action tokenizer discretizes continuous action chunks into tokens, which the policy generates either one token at time (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025) or in blocks of tokens predicted in parallel (Liu et al., 2026a; Jawaid and Xiang, 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). The action tokenizer thus determines what the policy learns to predict and how errors in those predictions affect the resulting robot motion (Pertsch et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2026). Existing tokenizers have explored frequency-domain compression (Pertsch et al., 2025), learned temporal abstraction (Mete et al., 2024), vector quantization (van den Oord et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025), and coarse-to-fine coding (Liu et al., 2026a; Jawaid and Xiang, 2026), but they treat an action chunk as flat vector and do not model how its dimensions are organized across the arms of the robot. This limitation is especially consequential in bimanual manipulation, where successful execution depends on coordinated motion across both arms. Tasks such as handing over objects, folding fabric, and carrying large objects often require two arms (Smith et al., 2012; Krebs and Asfour, 2022), and VLAs are increasingly being applied to these tasks (Liu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). However, most general-purpose action tokenizers concatenate both arms actions into single vector, formulation we call joint tokenization. Although this formulation can capture cross-arm dependencies, it leaves the structure of bimanual coordination to be learned implicitly. Human bimanual manipulation illustrates two useful aspects of this structure: the arms share repertoire of movements, yet adapt their actions to complementary roles (Guiard, 1987). During handover, for example, one hand presents and releases the object while the other reaches to receive and secure it. For robots with matching arm kinematics, this suggests an action representation that captures both reusable motion patterns across arms and task-dependent coordination between them. Joint tokenization does not explicitly distinguish these two aspects, leaving the policy to learn both shared motion structure and cross-arm dependencies from the concatenated representation. Making this structure explicit raises design question. One option, which we call per-arm tokenization, splits the action by arm and tokenizes each arm separately, as in M2Tok (Xu et al., 2026), leaving coordination to the policy. Per-arm tokenization yields arm-indexed tokens and lets both arms reuse one motion representation, but it removes partner context from each arms codes; in our experiments, such tokenizer performs no better than the strongest joint tokenizer (Sec. 4.2). This paper therefore asks: once the arms are tokenized as separate streams, how should the streams interact to yield better interface for bimanual policies? Our key insight is that arm-indexed tokens need not be arm-independent: each arms tokens can be computed with access to its partner while the two streams remain separate. We build on this insight in Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), per-arm tokenizer that restores partner context. Its design follows one principle: share the motion representation across arms while conditioning discretization on the partner arm. For the shared motion patterns, BiCAT exploits the mirror-image mounting of the arms: it maps the right arm into the left arms convention, so that mirrored motions share one canonical trajectory, and encodes both arms with one shared causal temporal encoder. For the cross-arm coordination, symmetric cross-arm attention adds partner context to each stream before shared finite scalar quantization (FSQ) (Mentzer et al., 2024), and joint decoder reconstructs both trajectories from temporally paired codes. Trained by reconstruction alone, BiCAT produces separate tokens for each arm, which the VLA predicts in two successive blocks: the tokens of each arm are generated in parallel, and the right arm is conditioned on the left. We compare BiCAT with eight baselines from seven tokenizer families under common VLA training protocol. On ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (Chen et al., 2026), BiCAT improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest baseline, with gain that grows from 1.5 points on single-arm tasks to 21.3 on tightly coupled ones, and on six real-world tasks across three embodiments it succeeds in 113 of 150 trials, compared with 74 for OAT (Liu et al., 2026a). Two-block prediction keeps policy latency at least 5.6 lower than token-by-token decoding. Ablations show that the gain requires both the tokenizer and the prediction schedule: removing cross-arm interaction or predicting both arms in one block leaves BiCAT no better than the strongest baseline. 2 Our contributions are threefold: BiCAT, per-arm action tokenizer that shares one motion representation across mirrored arms and exchanges partner context on both sides of the discrete bottleneck. Improved bimanual VLA control over eight baselines from seven tokenizer families in simulation, and over FAST and OAT on three real embodiments. An analysis of per-arm tokenization showing that cross-arm interaction inside the tokenizer and arm-wise block prediction in the policy are jointly required for the gain over joint tokenization.

sections.title:
2.2 Action Tokenization
Early discrete-action VLAs such as RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023;
Kim et al., 2024) discretize each action dimension into bins and predict the resulting symbols autoregressively,
which yields long sequences as the action dimension and horizon grow. FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025) shortens
them with a discrete cosine transform (DCT) and byte-pair encoding (BPE), at the cost of variable-length
sequences that can decode into invalid actions (Liu et al., 2026a). Learned tokenizers instead compress
action chunks into fixed sets of latent symbols: VQ-BeT (Lee et al., 2024b) and VQ-VLA (Wang et al.,
2025) use vector quantization, QueST (Mete et al., 2024) combines causal temporal encoding with finite
scalar quantization (Mentzer et al., 2024), and OAT (Liu et al., 2026a), NAC (Jawaid and Xiang, 2026), and
CATok (Zhang et al., 2026) order their tokens from coarse to fine.
sections.content: Beyond compression and reconstruction fidelity, recent work has examined how action representations affect downstream policy learning. ActionCodec (Dong et al., 2026) investigates tokenizer properties associated with VLA optimization, while X-Tokenizer (Kang et al., 2026) and ActionPiece (Lian et al., 2026) incorporate vision-language alignment and relational supervision between action chunks, respectively. When applied to bimanual robots, most existing discrete tokenizers operate on the concatenated action vector of both arms, the joint tokenization of Sec. 1. M2Tok (Xu et al., 2026) expands quantization capacity through multiple codebooks and tokenizes each arm separately, but does not model cross-arm interaction within the tokenizer, leaving its role in discrete action representations largely unexplored.

sections.title:
2.3 Bimanual Action Representations
Bimanual policies typically represent both arms as one concatenated action vector. ACT (Zhao et al., 2023)
and ALOHA Unleashed (Zhao et al., 2024) learn bimanual skills through action-chunk prediction, RDT-1B (Liu
et al., 2025) develops a large-scale diffusion policy for bimanual manipulation, and general-purpose VLAs

Explicit inter-arm structure has mainly been introduced in the policy: InterACT (Lee et al., 2024a) adds synchronization blocks between arm decoders. In the tokenizer, M2Tok (Xu et al., 2026) separates the arms but keeps them independent. BiCAT instead models cross-arm interaction within learned discrete action tokenizer, producing arm-indexed tokens through cross-arm attention and joint reconstruction.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: BiCAT tokenizes bimanual action chunk into two arm-indexed token streams that share one motion representation and are computed with access to each other  (Fig. 2)  . Sec. 3.1 introduces action tokenization in the bimanual setting, Sec. 3.2 describes the tokenizer, whose training is summarized in Algorithm 1, and Sec. 3.3 describes how VLA predicts its tokens.

sections.title:
3.3 Policy Training
After tokenizer training, we freeze BiCAT and use its tokens to supervise a pretrained VLM backbone with
parameters θV: PaliGemma 2-3B (Steiner et al., 2024) in simulation and Molmo2-ER (Fang et al., 2026) on
real robots (Sec. 4). The observation o forms the input prefix. We augment the vocabulary with K action
symbols and an input-only mask token (Chang et al., 2022).
sections.content: 6 Semi-autoregressive action prediction. Following semi-autoregressive decoding (Wang et al., 2018), the policy instantiates Eq. (1) with the two arm streams as successive blocks: pθV (y o) = pθV (yL o)pθV (yR o, yL). (10) The = 8 tokens within each arm block are predicted in parallel, and the right-arm block is conditioned on the complete left-arm block. During training, the input suffix ([MASK]M , yL) predicts (yL, yR) under block-causal attention. This lets the right block use the complete ground-truth left block without exposing its own targets. Both blocks receive equally weighted cross-entropy supervision LCE in one forward pass. At inference, two sequential block predictions generate the action tokens, and the frozen decoder reconstructs the continuous chunk. We use greedy decoding restricted to action symbols.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate BiCAT in simulation (Secs. 4.14.2) and on real robots (Sec. 4.3). Our experiments assess both downstream policy performance and, through controlled ablations, the impact of the key design choices of BiCAT.

sections.title:
4.1 Simulation Setup
Benchmark and protocol. RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2026) comprises 50 bimanual manipulation tasks.
Tokenizers and policies are trained on all 2,500 demonstrations from all 50 tasks. Each learned tokenizer is
pretrained with its own objective and then frozen, and a PaliGemma 2-3B backbone (Steiner et al., 2024) is
fully fine-tuned to predict its action tokens from a language instruction, the discretized robot state, and three
RGB views. Policies predict 32-step chunks and execute the first 16 before replanning. As many of these
tasks need only one arm, we evaluate on ten representative tasks, selected before training to cover three levels
of inter-arm coupling, inspired by the coordination taxonomy of Sa et al. (2026): two single-arm tasks, four
loosely coupled tasks where both arms act largely independently, and four tightly coupled tasks where each
arm’s motion depends on its partner (Appendix A). We report success over 100 rollouts per task and the
ten-task mean (settings in Appendix B).
sections.content: Baselines. We compare BiCAT with Bin (Kim et al., 2024), FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025), QueST (Mete et al., 2024), OAT (Liu et al., 2026a) with token-wise (OATsing) and five-block (OATpow2) prediction, M2Tok (Xu et al., 2026), NAC (Jawaid and Xiang, 2026), and ActionCodec (Dong et al., 2026); Table 1 lists their token budgets, vocabularies, sizes, prediction schedules, and latencies. To keep the comparison controlled, all learned tokenizers use vocabulary of 1920 or 2048 codes, 16 tokens per chunk except NAC (24, following its multi-scale design), and between 7.4M and 11.9M parameters, with BiCAT the smallest. All tokenizers are fitted or trained on the RoboTwin training data; FAST is refitted rather than taken from its released universal tokenizer, and M2Tok uses its released implementation (Appendix B.3). All methods share the data, backbone, observations, and optimization settings and differ only in the tokenizer and its prediction schedule.

sections.title:
4.2 Simulation Results and Analysis
We use RoboTwin 2.0 to answer four research questions. (Q1) Does building bimanual structure into the
tokenizer improve bimanual VLA control over existing tokenizers? (Q2) Where does the improvement come
from? (Q3) How sensitive is BiCAT to its vocabulary size, and where does it fall short? (Q4) What does
two-block prediction cost at inference time?
sections.content: Q1: How does BiCAT compare with baselines? As shown in Table 2, BiCAT reaches mean success rate of 69.3%, compared with 51.7% for NAC, the strongest baseline. The gain of 17.6 percentage points is accompanied by the best or tied-best result on eight of the ten tasks, and it grows with inter-arm coupling: over the strongest baseline in each group, BiCAT gains 1.5 points on the near-saturated single-arm tasks, 17.5 on loosely coupled tasks, and 21.3 on tightly coupled tasks. Since the learned tokenizers have comparable token budgets (Sec. 4.1), the gain is not explained by shorter action sequence. Q2: What explains the gains? Figure 3 relates mean success to six properties of each tokenizer and its trained policy. Consistent with ActionCodec (Dong et al., 2026), reconstruction fidelity does not predict control (ρ16 = 0.13): Bin and FAST reconstruct actions most accurately yet perform worst. Token accuracy is also uninformative (ρ9 = 0.42), as it is not comparable across vocabularies. Success instead tracks reliance on visual input (ρ16 = 0.72), consistency across replanning (ρ16 = 0.80), and smoothness at chunk boundaries (ρ16 = 0.78), and less closely tolerance to token errors (ρ16 = 0.51); BiCAT has the smallest boundary jump among the nine tokenizers. As eight of the 16 points are BiCAT or its variants, we read these correlations as descriptive rather than causal. Q2: Which components contribute? Table 3 ablates the design principle and the prediction schedule. Raw coordinates sets = 1, so the two arms share features for identical joint values rather than for mirrored motions, and motion such as reaching inward is encoded differently for each arm; Arm-specific modules gives each arm its own modules and normalization bounds. These variants lower success to 58.7% and 56.9%; sharing aligns the latents of the two arms (leftright MMD of 0.088 for BiCAT, versus 0.193 and 0.286; Appendix D). Removing the pre-quantization cross-attention (Decoder-only coupling), joint decoding (Encoder-only coupling), or both (Independent arms, controlled per-arm variant) lowers success to 51.7%, 56.0%, and 50.0%. The two interactions are complementary: each adds far more when the other is present (17.6 versus 6.0 points for cross-attention, 13.3 versus 1.7 for joint decoding), and removing them weakens error tolerance and visual grounding. Predicting both arms in one block (Single-block prediction) lowers success to 51.1%, so neither partner-aware codes without the arm-wise schedule nor the schedule without partner-aware codes exceeds NAC. FSQ Levels Induced [8,6,5] 240 [8,8,8] 512 [8,5,5,5] 1000 [8,8,6,5] 1920 [7,5,5,5,5] Mean SR 0.470 0.617 0.631 0.693 0. Q3: How does the vocabulary affect control? Table 4 varies the FSQ levels of BiCAT (per-task results in Appendix E). We choose the grids following FSQ (Mentzer et al., 2024): all levels satisfy Lj 5, and [8, 6, 5], [8, 5, 5, 5], and [7, 5, 5, 5, 5] are its recommended configurations for vocabularies of about 28, 210, and 212. Success rises from 47.0% with 240 codes to 69.3% with 1920 codes and falls to 58.9% with 4375 codes, so additional quantization capacity does not monotonically improve control, although changing the levels also changes the latent dimensionality. All other experiments use [8, 8, 6, 5], as do QueST and OAT. Q3: Where does BiCAT underperform? The improvement is not uniform. BiCAT reaches 88% on Handover Mic, below OATsing (94%) and QueST (90%), and 85% on Dump Bin Bigbin, below NAC (87%). On Handover Mic, four tokenizer ablations with the same block order reach 9296% (Appendix C), so this gap is not inherent to arm-wise tokens or two-block prediction. 9 Q4: What does two-block prediction cost? Table 1 reports per-chunk latency on one H200 GPU with batch size 1. Encoding and decoding take under 5 ms for every tokenizer, so latency is set by the prediction schedule. With two blocks, BiCAT takes 40.5 ms, comparable to M2Tok and NAC, which also predict two blocks, and 5.6 to over 11 faster than tokenizers decoded token by token. Only ActionCodec, which predicts single block, is faster (26.8 ms), but Single-block prediction costs BiCAT 18.2 points of success, so the second block is worth its extra decoding step.

Each row shows four keyframes of one task with short task description. Data and training. We collect 100 teleoperated demonstrations per task (105 for Pen). For each embodiment, one tokenizer is trained on all of its demonstrations and frozen, and one VLA policy with Molmo2-ER backbone (Fang et al., 2026) is trained on its tokens for all tasks of that embodiment. Within an embodiment, all methods use exactly the same data and training configuration, including training steps, learning rate, warmup, and batch size (Appendix F.1), and the final checkpoint is evaluated. Baselines and evaluation. We compare BiCAT with one representative tokenizer from each of the two main families: FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025), the widely adopted compression-based tokenizer, and OATsing (Liu et al., 2026a), learned tokenizer with ordered tokens and token-wise prediction. All policies run on one NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU and are evaluated for 25 trials per task, 150 per method. trial succeeds only if every stage of the task is completed, and the initial object placements are identical across methods. Inference latency is measured on YAM, from receiving an observation to outputting an action chunk, over all inference calls. The robot waits during inference, so latency lengthens an episode but does not change the observations on which chunks are predicted (Appendix F.2). Results. As shown in Table 5, BiCAT succeeds in 113 of 150 trials, compared with 74 for OATsing and 25 for FAST, leads on all six tasks, and has the lowest inference latency, 4.7 lower than FAST. Consistent with simulation, the advantage persists across physical bimanual embodiments.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion & Limitations
sections.content: We introduced BiCAT, bimanual action tokenizer for autoregressive VLAs that combines shared motion representation across mirrored arms with partner-conditioned discretization, while preserving separate token streams for each arm. The policy predicts these streams in two successive blocks, requiring only two decoding steps per action chunk. Across simulation and three real-world bimanual embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated tokenizers, with larger gains on tasks requiring tighter coordination. Ablations show that both cross-arm interaction within the tokenizer and blockwise prediction in the policy are necessary for these gains over joint tokenization, highlighting action tokenization as an effective way to model bimanual coordination. However, BiCAT currently operates in joint space: its fixed per-joint sign mapping does not directly extend to end-effector actions, which require different transformations for positions and orientations. Each tokenizer is also trained for single embodiment and assigns equal, fixed token budgets to both arms. Extending BiCAT to end-effector actions, cross-embodiment transfer, and adaptive token allocation remains future work.

A.1 Evaluation Protocol Each method is evaluated with 100 rollouts per task using different random seeds. We use RoboTwins task-specific success checks and report both per-task success and the unweighted mean across the ten tasks. Policies predict 32-step action chunks, execute the first 16 steps, and then replan from new observation. All ten evaluation tasks belong to the 50-task collection used for training.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: This section complements Sec. 4.1 with the simulation training details of BiCAT and the baselines. 15 B.1 Training Data and Inputs The 5% validation split is drawn at the episode level with fixed seed, giving 2,375 training and 125 validation episodes, and is shared by tokenizer and policy training. Action chunks of 32 steps are sampled within episode boundaries; each step has 14 dimensions, six joint values and one gripper value per arm. The three RGB views come from the head and the two wrist cameras, and the robot state is encoded as text prefix with 256 bins per dimension. All policies use the paligemma2-3b-mix-224 checkpoint. B.2 Optimization Settings Table 7 lists the optimization settings shared by all methods. Policies minimize teacher-forced action-token cross-entropy and use greedy decoding during evaluation. Table 7 Shared optimization settings for the simulation comparison. Tokenizer pretraining applies to QueST, both OAT variants, M2Tok, NAC, ActionCodec, and BiCAT. The policy learning rate applies equally to the language model, vision encoder, and modality bridge. Setting Optimizer steps Batch size Optimizer Learning rate Adam β Adam ϵ Weight decay Warmup steps Schedule after warmup Final learning rate Precision Gradient norm limit Validation interval Tokenizer pretraining 300k 512 AdamW 5 105 (0.9, 0.95) 108 0 200 Constant 5 105 BF16 1.0 1k steps Policy training 30k 64 AdamW 104 (0.95, 0.999) 106 106 500 Cosine 105 BF16 1.0 1k steps B.3 Tokenizer Configurations Table 1 in the main paper lists the token count, vocabulary size, and prediction schedule of each tokenizer. All learned tokenizers use hidden width of 256 unless noted and are trained on action reconstruction. Bin (Kim et al., 2024): each normalized action value is mapped to one of 256 uniform bins. FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025): discrete cosine transform, coefficient quantization, and byte-pair encoding, fitted on the RoboTwin training split rather than taken from the released universal tokenizer; it yields 26.8 tokens per chunk on average (range 980). QueST (Mete et al., 2024): causal temporal convolutions followed by six-layer causal Transformer encoder, with FSQ levels [8, 8, 6, 5]. OAT (Liu et al., 2026a): learned register tokens trained with nested prefix dropout over {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} registers, with FSQ levels [8, 8, 6, 5]; the two variants differ only in their register and prediction block schedules. M2Tok (Xu et al., 2026): the released implementation with width 120. shared convolutional VQ-VAE encodes each arm independently into two latent frames, each quantized by four cosine-similarity codebooks of 512 entries, and reconstructs each arm from its own tokens. NAC (Jawaid and Xiang, 2026): SEANet encoder over the time-major flattened chunk and two-level residual FSQ with levels [8, 8, 4, 4], coarse level of 8 tokens and fine level of 16; its Vocos decoder is trained with reconstruction, adversarial, and feature-matching losses. ActionCodec (Dong et al., 2026): six-layer Perceiver-style encoder and decoder, with 16 latent vectors quantized by 2048-entry VQ codebook updated by exponential moving average. 16 BiCAT: the architecture of Sec. 3, with one shared causal self-attention layer and one symmetric cross-arm attention layer in the encoder, FSQ levels [8, 8, 6, 5], and six-layer joint decoder. Per-Task Ablation Results Table 9 reports per-task success for the variants summarized in Table 3.

sections.title: D Shared Arm Representations
sections.content: Figure 6 visualizes the pre-quantization latents of BiCAT, Raw coordinates, and Arm-specific modules. We encode 10,000 action chunks from the ten evaluation tasks, average each arms eight pre-quantization latent vectors, and embed the leftand right-arm averages of each model jointly with t-SNE. With all modules shared, the latents of the two arms overlap. With Arm-specific modules, the two arms occupy largely separate regions, so the shared FSQ grid assigns the same token IDs to latents that are distributed differently for the two arms. We quantify the overlap with the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the leftand right-arm averages in the original 4-D latent space, using an RBF kernel whose bandwidth is the median pairwise squared distance. The MMD is 0.088 for BiCAT, 0.193 for Raw coordinates, and 0.286 for Arm-specific modules, and the ordering is unchanged after pooled per-dimension standardization. Under Raw coordinates, the two arms remain visually mixed in the t-SNE embedding, yet their MMD is more than twice that of BiCAT, so canonicalization aligns the arms beyond what the shared encoder alone achieves. These distances describe arm-marginal distributions: they are consistent with, but do not directly measure, token ID denoting the same motion for both arms, and they do not by themselves measure coordination or task success. Per-Task FSQ Ablation Table 10 reports per-task success for the FSQ grids summarized in Table 4. All grids use the BiCAT architecture and the common training and evaluation protocol. Real-World Experiment Details Table 11 lists the six real-world tasks. All demonstrations are collected by teleoperation and recorded at 30 Hz, which is also the control frequency at deployment. F.1 Training Settings Table 8 Real-world optimizer steps per embodiment. All tokenizers on the same embodiment use the same numbers of steps. Embodiment Tokenizer steps Policy steps Bimanual SO-101 Unitree G1 Bimanual YAM 50k 80k 300k 4k 9k 20k Each embodiment is trained separately. For each embodiment, one action tokenizer is trained on the demonstrations of all its tasks in Table 11 without held-out validation split and then frozen, and one VLA policy is trained on its tokens jointly for all of these tasks; on Unitree G1, for example, single tokenizer and single policy cover both Bottle and Bowl. Table 8 lists the numbers of optimizer steps, which scale with the amount of data on each embodiment. BiCAT and OATsing use the same tokenizer architectures as in simulation, with 16 tokens per chunk and FSQ levels [8, 8, 6, 5], and FAST is fitted separately on the demonstrations of each embodiment. 17 Policy. The real-world policies use Molmo2-ER (Fang et al., 2026) as the vision-language backbone, which is fully fine-tuned together with the vision encoder and the modality bridge. The policy observes the language instruction, the joint state of both arms, and three RGB views from the current time step: top camera and the two wrist cameras. On Bimanual YAM and Unitree G1 the top view has resolution of 360 640 and the wrist views 480 640; on Bimanual SO-101 all three views are 480 640. The policy predicts 32-step action chunks as in simulation, but on the real robots it executes all 32 steps of each chunk before replanning, rather than the first 16. Optimization. Tokenizer pretraining uses the settings of Table 7 except for the number of steps  (Table 8)  . Policy training uses the same peak learning rate and cosine decay as in simulation, with global batch size of 128, BF16 mixed precision, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. Within an embodiment, the training configuration is identical across methods: BiCAT and OATsing are trained for the same number of tokenizer steps, FAST is fitted on the same demonstrations, and all three policies share the data, observations, number of policy steps, learning rate, warmup, and batch size. They differ only in the tokenizer and its prediction schedule. F.2 Evaluation Protocol Each method is evaluated for 25 trials per task. trial counts as success only if the robot completes every stage of the task without error; on Block, for example, the block must be placed in the box and the box handed over. Partial completion counts as failure. During deployment, the robot waits while the policy predicts the next action chunk and executes the chunk once inference has finished, so differences in inference latency lengthen the episode but do not change the observation on which each chunk is predicted. The initial object placements are identical across methods for each trial, and each trial is limited to 120 s, after which it counts as failure. Inference latency is measured from receiving an observation to outputting an action chunk, over all inference calls during the YAM evaluation, and is reported as mean standard deviation.
